inuit.publisher: Inuit Art Foundation / Inuit Art Quarterly; Elaine Anselmi
inuit.readScope: Complete actual feature body read, online June 16, 2021, originally Winter 2019, including Lydia Qayaq interview and attributed quarry report. No artwork/photo inspected.
inuit.role: Named Inuit carver's knowledge of harder/softer stone and material selection; specific locality, artist and report attribution retained. No blanket soapstone assumption, legal entitlement lesson or child quarry/carving task.

classification.sourceSummary: Mineral composition, rock constituents and physical texture/property evidence are different classification criteria. Granite and some sandstone can share quartz/feldspar/mica but arrange them differently; calcite can vary in colour.
classification.attributionLimits: Prepared known reference entries and adult-approved specimens; an unknown rock cannot be confidently identified from colour alone. No claim a scratch test determines exact chemical composition.
classification.question: Original reference tray: G is coarse interlocking granite with quartz/feldspar/mica; S is a sandstone with grains of those same named minerals cemented together; Q is a labelled quartz mineral specimen; C1 and C2 are known calcite samples with different colours; M is known mica. Adult supplies intact safe specimens and reference composition cards. Observe with lens and record texture, grain/crystal appearance, colour and lustre; compare scratch resistance only with an adult-approved safe kit. Sort/re-sort by at least two tested physical criteria, then separately group by supplied composition (single mineral/aggregate, quartz-containing and mica-containing groups can overlap).
classification.expectedEvidence: Record actual observations rather than invent values. Use the composition cards to distinguish constituent knowledge from appearance: granite and sandstone may share constituents but differ in grain arrangement/formation; differently coloured calcite belongs to the same known mineral identity. Explain overlaps and compare two specimens using more than colour. Mineral properties/identity constrain a classification; they do not make every similar-looking specimen the same material.
classification.nearMiss: Infers composition from colour, calls every crystalline rock igneous or assumes one specimen can belong to only one valid grouping.
classification.changedCase: Replace one colour of calcite with another known calcite and a similar-coloured quartz: retain/revise the composition grouping using references and test evidence. For an unlabelled sample say what further evidence is needed, rather than guess confidently.

haida-selection.sourceSummary: The museum account identifies a particular Haida argillite source and explains that the soft but fragile stone responds to carving tools.
haida-selection.attributionLimits: Museum attribution remains explicit. Particular Haida practice, not all First Nations; no copying crest/origin-story designs, quarrying or carving protected materials.
haida-selection.question: Use the selected account to explain how workability and fragility help a Haida carver select and handle this material for a detailed sculpture. Contrast with an original brief requiring a hard-wearing step stone; can one desirable property determine both choices?
haida-selection.expectedEvidence: Relate learned material qualities and carver knowledge to a particular purpose; a workable stone may need careful handling. Explain why a sculpture choice does not automatically suit a load-bearing/wear purpose.
haida-selection.nearMiss: Names a people or decorative object without connecting the selected rock's properties to purpose, or treats every black rock as this particular argillite.
haida-selection.changedCase: An original supplied stone looks similar but crumbles under the proposed fine detail: explain why appearance alone does not establish suitability and why the expert/source distinction matters.

metis-selection.sourceSummary: Rupertsland describes Métis firebags carrying flint and steel for fire-starting; the separate NPS account explains hot metal particles removed using a suitable hard stone edge.
metis-selection.attributionLimits: Two differently attributed sources supply cultural use and material mechanism. This does not claim Métis knowledge is reducible to the NPS explanation or that every community used identical equipment. No fire-making, gunpowder, tobacco activity or artifact handling.
metis-selection.question: Read the Métis-authored purpose account alongside the separately attributed mechanism summary. Explain why carrying a suitable flint edge and steel is purpose-related material selection rather than choosing any attractive pebble. An original fictional substitute is soft and rounds off without producing the required metal particles: explain why it would not meet this particular brief.
metis-selection.expectedEvidence: Connect the described material pairing/edge property to the intended fire-starting function and keep each source's contribution distinct. Explain that the sparks in this supplied flint-and-steel mechanism are heated metal particles, not the rock turning into fire.
metis-selection.nearMiss: Only describes the bag's decoration, claims all rock burns or presents the US source as the Métis-authored cultural account.
metis-selection.changedCase: For a changed original brief of carving fine detail rather than fire-starting, reconsider which properties matter; no cultural ranking or practical test with sparks.

inuit-selection.sourceSummary: The feature reports Lydia Qayaq's expert distinction between harder/softer stone and work with marble; its attributed quarry report values consistency, toughness, fine detail and polish.
inuit-selection.attributionLimits: Artist interview and cited report are distinct voices. Material names and practices vary by place/person; do not equate all Inuit carving with soapstone or infer novices can diagnose stone by colour alone.
inuit-selection.question: Use the named interview/report summaries to explain how a carver's knowledge of stone and intended carving informs selection. Compare detail, toughness, finish and access constraints using the actual source; distinguish expert observation from a novice colour guess.
inuit-selection.expectedEvidence: Explain at least two material-quality/purpose connections, including the trade-off that easiest to mark is not automatically most suitable for a durable detailed carving. Retain the artist/locality and report attributions.
inuit-selection.nearMiss: Labels all carving stone soapstone or treats colour alone as a universal identification test.
inuit-selection.changedCase: The original brief changes from a polished detailed carving to a rough low-detail model, or the available block has cracks: explain how the purpose/quality comparison changes and what expert information remains needed.

wholeClaimReview.readScope: Complete R6/wH cards and 3-card/2-edge hard closure read. Complete R6 saved guide read; wH has no guide. Existing rock-type and rock-cycle cards/guides also read during overall preparation; no changed claim/guide/age/edge.
limits: R6 supplies actual rock-property comparison and sorting, not exact chemical identification by colour/scratch alone.
wH supplies mineral-property/resource-use components. Its explicit Australian resource example remains a whole-claim requirement; a Canadian case is not silently substituted.

The prepared portfolio supplies actual source-specific composition and community material-selection evidence. Neither identity recognition, generic respect nor a previous property score certifies E2.6. No fixed memorised cultural case inventory is imposed.

safety: Adult chooses known intact nonhazardous educational specimens, safe rounded equipment and school procedures. No dust generation, breaking/carving stone, tasting/licking/smelling, strong acid, unknown mineral collection, fire/sparks or handling cultural artifacts. Textual cases do not claim practical performance occurred.
